content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a retrieval strategy based on learning from text triplet representations of relations in a Knowledge Graph and corresponding/aligned descriptive text. The authors reference this as a "cross-modal" learning and retrieval strategy.  The authors evaluate this triplet/RDF-to-text model using standard retrieval datasets and recall metrics, while also introducing a reference free evaluation strategy leveraging the text embeddings learned from this joint model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- this paper is fairly well written and easy to follow.
- the authors do a good job in exploring a data augmentation strategy using corrupted triples as a means to gauge robustness of their proposed approach.

Weakness:
- the authors use a baseline that i am not sure why is even a competing baseline. The baseline used is a sentence encoder that understandably never took RDF data as an input, so I am not sure why is this even a competing baseline.
- similarly, though the datasets appear disparate, they all ingest Wikipedia data or map to Wikipedia one way. or the other, due to this, in my opinion apart from TREx, it is unclear exactly how the other two datasets are complimentary.
- empirical comparisons and baselines seem weak. 
-writing has some missing references that show up as "?" in the manuscript.
- Not entirely sure how authors would handle scenarios with no parallel data
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I was a little thrown off with the use of the term "cross-modal", since I was interpreting this as a "text-image", "text-audio" or "audio-image" style of joint learning. Regardless, this is a minor nit. Despite learning from a KB both "modalities" are in text, so this use of terminology just feels off. 

While the premise is promising, I am not sure the experiments are novel enough. For instance, the baseline the authors compare against is a sentence transformer that is trained on text, and on which their models are trained. This right away sets the baseline up for failure! The authors should have atleast considered other sentence/text encoders or should have pooled the output of token level encoders at least. 

Furthermore most of the training datasets leverage triplet information to obtain the aligned text, particularly like in KELM where the triplets are fed to a T5 model to generate text. Now the authors propose using the generated text and and triplets (used to generate the text) to learn a joint representations, I am not entirely sure how this is not redundant.
content.summary_of_the_review:
While the authors propose an interesting idea to combine RDF representation of knowledge graphs and use aligned text to learn better joint embeddings, I find the empirical evaluations, baseline and choice of datasets as insufficient in establishing the authors' hypothesis.
A lot of these results are conditioned on the availability of parallel text. Furthermore, the choice of baseline seems very naive.
An interesting result would be one where the authors leverage similar text in addition to corrupted triples to impute joint embeddings and evaluate their retrieval performance.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper examines approaches to learn to align RDF and text data. It describes a series of methods to improve the alignment, including using a combination of datasets, using bi-encoder and ensembling. Finally, the resulting similarity measure by the model is proposed as an evaluation metric. Compared to other automatic metrics, the proposed one is shown to have a better correlation with human evaluation metrics.
The main contribution of the paper is about the cross-modal similarity between RDF data and texts.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper describes detailed steps in an attempt to better align RDF data with the corresponding text. There are several related approaches trying to align different types of data (e.g. image and text). This paper follows the same general idea, i.e. representations are built for RDF and text data, either separately or jointly, then their relationship is determined by a classifier or by cosine similarity. The new aspect of this paper is that it looks at RDF-text data.
In terms of methods, the methods are existing ones. The authors tested a series of existing methods to select the one that fits the best the test data. This include the selection of encoding method, the similarity measure and the training data. This series of tests and selections is not new. They correspond to a series of tests that one should normally do for most tasks. What would be interesting is to provide some insights along with the process. Unfortunately, the paper does not provide in-depth analysis for that. So, the value of this series of tests is limited.
The second part of the paper is about using the similarity measure as an evaluation metric. While it is interesting to see a stronger correlation of this measure with human evaluations, it is difficult to propose the model as a metric. This would depend strongly on the training data etc. A better trained model would likely lead to a stronger correlation. So, at the end, one is not testing what metric is more reasonable, but how the model that produces the metric should be trained. The observation made in the paper is limited to the training data and the model used. It is difficult to generalize. The overall conclusion of the paper is unclear.
The paper suffers from a lack of organization. The authors are content to describe the experiments carried out, without providing the intended goal and the insights. It is quite boring to read this paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The description is not well structured. The novelty of the paper is limited to testing on RDF-text data, with the existing methods. The novelty is very limited.The code and the (sub)dataset used are not made available. The reproduction of the result is difficult.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper describes a series of test and attempts without a good structure. The proposed metric may not be applicable in general. The contribution of the paper is limited.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the text and knowledge graph retrieval task. Specifically, given a dataset with aligned text and knowledge graph, the model is required to produce a higher similarity score for the aligned pairs. The unaligned pairs should receive a lower score. The author claims that by jointly training on multiple text-knowledge graph dataset, the model could achieve higher performance than the previous state-of-the-art which is only trained on text only data. The author also finds that the learned text-knowledge graph model can be used for evaluating the knowledge graph to text generation task.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
1. Admittedly, this paper achieves higher performance than the previous approach. But I wonder what is the technical novelty of this paper? Furthermore, what is the scientific novelty of this paper?
2. What is the motivation of doing the knowledge graph and text retrieval task? The introduction didn't explain nor illustrate the motivation of this paper.
3. IIUC, the proposed approach is a dual encoder that encodes the text and knowledge graph as embeddings. Then the contrastive loss is conducted for learning the embeddings. If so, I wonder could the author explain in details of how to encode the knowledge graph as input for the encoder?
4. The paper is hastily written. The paper is not smooth to read.
5. What is the meaning of 'allows us both to leverage' in introduction?
6. What is the meaning of "to inferface with text data"?
7. I wonder whether the comparison against the previous state-of-the-art is fair. IIUC, the previous state-of-the-art model is a text based approach, which is not trained on text-knowledge graph dataset. While the proposed approach is trained on the text-knowledge graph dataset. It Is natural that the proposed approach achieves higher performance than the previous state-of-the-art. If both models are trained on the same dataset, it will then be considered as a fair comparison.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I think the paper is hastily written. The writing actually negatively affect the understanding of this paper.
I wonder what is the novelty of this paper. As this paper is more like a experimental report rather than a scientific paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the writing quality and the lack of novelty, I would recommend reject at current stage.

content.title: Joint Representations of Text and Knowledge Graphs for Retrieval and Evaluation
content.TL;DR: We learn joint representations for knowledge base elements and corresponding text, which allows to perform retrieval and referenceless adequacy evaluation
content.abstract: A key feature of neural models is that they can produce semantic vector representations of objects (texts, images, speech, etc.) ensuring that similar objects are close to each other in the vector space. While much work has focused on learning text, image, knowledge-base (KB) and image-text representations, there are no aligned cross-modal text-KB representations. One challenge for learning such representations is the lack of parallel data. We train retrieval models on datasets  of (graph, text) pairs where the graph is a KB subgraph and the text has been heuristically aligned with the graph. When performing retrieval on WebNLG, a clean parallel corpus, our best model achieves 80\% accuracy and 99\% recall@10, showing that similar texts and KB graphs are mapped close to each other. We use this property to create a similarity metric between English text and KB graphs, matching state-of-the-art metrics in terms of correlation with human judgments even though, unlike them, it does not require a reference text to compare against.
